clue.text: Shifts are run up for all — 1, cerements here too!

indicators.note: shifts as a verb means moves things about, so the letters of the preceding words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Everyone has their shifts run up, and shrouds are made here as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shifts' looks like a noun for garments, fitting the cerements, but it is the anagram signal working on ARE RUN UP FOR ALL.
explanation.definitionFit: Cerements are burial shrouds, and an undertaker's premises is where bodies are dressed in them.

clue.text: Caught in running from the MIG and other planes?

indicators.note: the letter for caught is placed inside the rearranged letters
running suggests something in motion and disorder, so the letters are shuffled

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A question about which aircraft were caught while fleeing the Soviet jet.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures fleeing a Soviet jet. FIGHTER COMMAND was the RAF branch flying Spitfires and Hurricanes, Britain's own planes as against the MiG.
explanation.definitionFit: The RAF's wartime fighter arm flew British aircraft, a different set of warplanes from the Soviet jet mentioned.

clue.text: European never wearing slacks?

parts.note: no in the sense of 'not at all, never' as in 'no way'

indicators.note: slacks as a verb means loosens, so the letters of the preceding word come loose and rearrange

explanation.surface: Asks whether a continental is someone who refuses to wear trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slacks' looks like trousers being worn, but it is a verb telling you to rearrange WEARING into RWEGIAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from Norway is a Scandinavian and so a native of Europe.

clue.text: Leads to 'rail', hale 'and Yale' taking endings in poem? True!

definitions.text: Leads to 'rail', hale 'and Yale' taking endings in poem? True!

indicators.note: the leads of words are their opening letters, so the first letters of the three quoted words are taken
endings point to the final letters of the two words that follow

explanation.surface: A mock-cockney chant of rhyming words, then a claim that this is how a poem works.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letters of rail, hale and Yale give RHY and the last letters of poem and True give ME. The quoted words themselves chime, so the whole clue also defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Words like rail, hale and Yale share their sound endings, the matching device found in verse.

clue.text: Cure vital in treatment is very profitable

indicators.note: being treated means being worked on and altered, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A vital cure, used in therapy, makes a lot of money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in treatment' rearranges CURE VITAL; the medical surface hides the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucrative work brings in a great deal of money, the same idea as highly profitable.

clue.text: See 1
Choose to receive start of remedy in injection

indicators.note: one word receiving a letter means it holds that letter inside it

parts.note: to choose is to pick

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Decide to have a dose of medicine given by needle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to receive' puts R (the start of 'remedy') inside PICK.
explanation.definitionFit: A prick is a small puncture, as made by a needle when giving a jab.

clue.text: Economic activity in narrative's fine

indicators.note: the letter for fine goes inside the word for a story

parts.note: a relation is a telling or account, a narrative
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine

explanation.surface: A remark that business is going well in a story.
explanation.walkthrough: F (fine) goes inside RELATION, an old word for a narrative.
explanation.definitionFit: Reflation is a stimulus to a country's money supply and spending to expand output, a form of economic policy.

clue.text: Japanese city, large with indication of alternative name

parts.note: OS stands for outsize, a clothing label for large
AKA, short for 'also known as', introduces another name

explanation.surface: A big Japanese place that goes by another name too.
explanation.definitionFit: Osaka is a major port on Honshu, Japan's second metropolis after Tokyo.

clue.text: Darning singlets for marathon entrants?

parts.note: mending vests worn by long-distance racers is literally a fix made by and for those who run; the phrase normally means quick fixes made while something keeps working

explanation.surface: Sewing up the vests of people taking part in a long race.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means minor fixes done without stopping operation, and here it is read as mending the kit of race competitors.

clue.text: Gaily eating recipe — not one like cheesecake?

indicators.note: one word eating a letter takes it inside
not one means the letter for one is removed

parts.note: A is one, as in a single
R is the abbreviation for recipe, from Latin 'take'

explanation.surface: Someone happily eats from a recipe, but this is not a cheesecake.
explanation.walkthrough: GAILY loses A ('not one') to give GILY, which is 'eating' R. Cheesecake here is slang for pin-up pictures of women.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheesecake is glamour photography of women, and girly magazines are full of such pin-ups.

clue.text: Principal metal casing a tank

parts.note: a principal is a chief or head

indicators.note: one word casing another wraps around it

parts.note: tin is a metal

explanation.surface: The head of a company's metal works encasing an armoured vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: CHIEF, then TIN 'casing' A. The Chieftain was a British main battle tank.
explanation.definitionFit: The Chieftain was a British Army armoured fighting vehicle in service from the 1960s.

clue.text: Tourist trap showing record investing in the currency

indicators.note: investing here means clothing or enclosing, so one piece is wrapped around another

parts.note: the mark was the German currency
EP, extended play, is a kind of record

explanation.surface: A tourist trap shows a record being invested in money.
explanation.walkthrough: The financial surface hides 'investing' in its old sense of clothing or wrapping round. The mark was Germany's currency before the euro.
explanation.definitionFit: An amusement park built around a single subject draws crowds of visitors and their money.

clue.text: Calculators helping to make arithmetic a ball, on reflection

indicators.note: reflection in a mirror flips things, so the letters run backwards
the letters help make up the words, so they are found within the run arithmetic a ball

explanation.surface: Gadgets that make sums fun, when you think about it.
explanation.walkthrough: Inside 'arithmetIC A BAll' sits ICABA; 'on reflection' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: These bead frames are counting devices, plural of the word for a single such frame.

clue.text: Regretting one cutting into support for feet

indicators.note: one piece cutting into another sits inside it

parts.note: the rung of a ladder holds the feet of a climber
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A person regrets the moment a ladder step breaks under them.
explanation.walkthrough: I 'cutting into' RUNG. 'Support for feet' suggests a footrest or shoe, but it is the step of a ladder.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruing is feeling sorry about something done, being remorseful.

clue.text: Odd signals work — sound of a trombone, say

indicators.note: work as a verb means knead or shape, so the letters are reformed

parts.note: the setter meant 'Od signals', whose letters are shuffled; as printed one D is surplus

explanation.surface: Strange messages give out a brassy note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'work' rearranges the fodder, but as printed 'Odd signals' has one D too many; it presumably should read 'Od signals'.
explanation.definitionFit: A glissando is a slide between pitches, the trademark swoop a trombone's slide makes.

clue.text: Thinking I'm in The Gorgon's Head imbibing a drink

indicators.note: imbibing means drinking in, so the following words go inside the preceding ones

parts.note: taken as written without the apostrophe
taken as written

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: gin is a drink

explanation.surface: Someone muses that they are inside Medusa's skull, sipping a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures someone inside Medusa's head; 'imbibing' puts A GIN after the first two letters of IMING (I'M, IN and the Gorgon's head G).
explanation.definitionFit: Imagining is conceiving or picturing in the mind, a kind of thought.

clue.text: Offering various wheezes when topical — no end of influence

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

indicators.note: no here means without, so the letter for the end of influence is removed

parts.note: thematic means relating to a topic or subject

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: Proposing assorted clever schemes when they are of the moment, though lacking clout.
explanation.walkthrough: AS, then THEMATIC with E (the 'end of influence') removed. 'Wheezes' looks like tricks or schemes; it is breathing sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A person with this lung condition produces whistling breaths when struggling for air.

clue.text: Unknown coin and ingot melted down

indicators.note: melting metal destroys its form, so the letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: Money and a bar of gold are melted into an anonymous lump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'melted down' rearranges COIN and INGOT; the metallurgy fits the surface neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone travelling under a false identity is unrecognised, not known for who they are.

clue.text: Against reversing if bump is assured

parts.note: con means against, as in pros and cons

indicators.note: reversing turns the short word round so it reads backwards

parts.note: a dent is a bump or knock in a surface

explanation.surface: A driver who backs into something with a bump is insured.
explanation.walkthrough: The motoring surface of a bump makes 'assured' look like insured; 'reversing' turns IF round.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-assured person is certain and poised, sure of themselves.

clue.text: See 1
New patissier's tool is more pleasing

parts.note: a pastry cook uses an icer to decorate cakes

explanation.surface: A pastry chef's new gadget is better.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicer is the comparative of nice, meaning more agreeable or delightful.

clue.text: See 8
End of piece in disarray? Supply of inspiration

indicators.note: the final letter is placed inside the word for disorder

parts.note: muss means a mess or disorder

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: Asks whether the finish of a work is chaotic, then offers creative ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: E (the 'End of piece') goes inside MUSS.
explanation.definitionFit: The nine Greek goddesses of the arts were the source from which poets drew their ideas.

clue.text: One in bed's laid up, showing fortitude

indicators.note: in a down clue, being laid up means placed upward, so the letters read from bottom to top
the numeral goes inside the word for small beds

parts.note: a cot is a bed; bed's read as cot's gives the letters
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone stuck in bed with an illness is bearing it bravely.
explanation.walkthrough: I goes 'in' COTS to make CIOTS, which 'laid up' turns upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A Stoic endures hardship without complaint, keeping calm courage.

clue.text: Arithmetic's more important, in conclusion

parts.note: summing is doing arithmetic, and the 's stands for 'is'
up means higher or ahead, as in being up on someone

explanation.surface: In the end, maths counts for more.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as 'summing is up': arithmetic has risen in importance.
explanation.definitionFit: A judge's or speaker's closing review of the points is the final part of a case or speech.

clue.text: Glasses for small amounts, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound-alike, so the word is spelt differently from how it sounds

parts.note: specks are tiny particles or bits

explanation.surface: Spectacles bought for a little money, so they say.
explanation.walkthrough: SPECKS (tiny bits) sounds like SPECS, slang for spectacles.
explanation.definitionFit: Specs is the informal short form for eyeglasses.

clue.text: One North American Republican's held in embrace

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: one piece held by another sits inside it

parts.note: R stands for Republican, the 's being 'is'

explanation.surface: A US politician from the north is clasped in a hug.
explanation.walkthrough: I, N, then R 'held' in AM. Inarm is an old poetic verb for hugging.
explanation.definitionFit: Inarm is an archaic literary verb meaning to clasp in one's arms, to hug.

clue.text: Sailors and soldiers in a spot will get decoration

indicators.note: the service personnel are placed inside the small mark

parts.note: a dot is a spot
RN is the Royal Navy, sailors
men are soldiers, as in officers and men

explanation.surface: Military personnel caught in a tight situation will be awarded a medal.
explanation.walkthrough: RN and MEN go 'in' A DOT. 'Decoration' suggests a medal, but means ornament.
explanation.definitionFit: Adornment is ornament or embellishment added to make something attractive.

clue.text: Excuse failure to be present?

definitions.meaning: a claim that clears someone of blame
the Latin origin means 'elsewhere', a plea that one was absent from the scene

explanation.definitionFit: A plea of having been somewhere else serves as a defence, and it literally rests on someone's absence from the crime.

clue.text: Historic legal group changes Parliament?

parts.note: to doctor something is to alter or tamper with it
the Commons is the lower house of the UK Parliament

explanation.surface: A long-established legal body reforms the legislature.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctors' Commons was a London society of civil lawyers, dissolved in the 19th century.
explanation.definitionFit: This London society of lawyers practising civil law existed for centuries until its abolition in 1865.

clue.text: See 27
